page.eyebrow: Two of Us · Home’s sky · round three
page.title: Miller’s hill
page.lede: This build has the fixes from the first review. Bedtime looks up and stays up, the night now lasts until first light, the moment is a second shorter, and the drawing has had a pass on an illustrator’s and an art director’s notes. One more pass is still to come. Start with the film.

feature.title: Bedtime, staying up
feature.sub: He goes down for the night at 7:40. Each film is the mockup stepped one frame at a time and joined, so the timing is as designed. It does not show how fast a phone will draw it.

bed: The view rises from the hill to the sky. Tonight’s star lifts off the tree’s shoulder with it.
A band of light leaves tonight’s star and crosses the sky. His stars answer as it passes, and the night’s number stands at the foot.
The cards return over the sky that is already there. Nothing looks back down.
Home stays looking up until first light.
arrive: A night sleep is logged from the other phone, Siri or the SNOO while Home is open.
The view rises quietly behind the cards and tonight’s star fades in. No band and no caption, and the cards stay where they are.
settle: First light, about 6:12 a.m. in late November, if Home is open.
The view comes down to the hill behind the cards, and tonight’s star goes out with the last of the stars.
If Home is closed at first light, it is back on the hill the next time you open it.
open: The closed phone’s sky is already on the right-hand page. The left page arrives bare.
By day, light runs down the river toward you. At night, the page’s stars come out from the fold.

page.nightTitle: The night, with the cards on
page.nightSub: Home from bedtime until first light, at 7:40, 9:00 and 3 a.m. Tonight’s star is the larger four-pointed one. A feed in the night shows the same sky. Switch the look and the display in the bar above.
page.bedtimeSub: The same moment as stills, to hold any instant. The cards step back, the view rises, the band crosses, and the cards return over the sky.
page.openSub: The closed phone’s sky is already on the right-hand page. The left page arrives bare, light runs down the river toward you, and then its cards land.

mine.title: What changed since the last build, and what is still open
paragraphs: The night lasts until first light. Home looks up from bedtime until the sky begins to lighten, about 6:12 a.m. in late November. A feed at 3 a.m. moves nothing, and waking no longer jumps. I took this from your “looking back down is too much”, and it is the one rule here you have not agreed to. The alternative is that the view comes down when he wakes. The film “First light” shows the one time the view does come down, quietly, behind the cards.
The moment is a second shorter: 5.8 seconds, down from 6.8. The time came out of the cards, which now leave in one second and return in 1.2. The sky keeps its pace.

Nothing is cut by a card’s edge when Home looks up. That has a cost. With the cards on at night, the closed Duo and an ordinary iPhone do not show the moon’s disc at all, because everywhere it would stand a card’s edge would cut it. It is still there in the bedtime moment, and briefly on the open Duo as it crosses the gap by the fold.

The drawing had its pass. An illustrator found the first round-three clouds too modelled and too loud, and the small one under the Wi-Fi and battery symbols read as a weather symbol. Clouds are now quiet flat banks, and that one is gone. The crowns in leaf are rounded masses, the river has no dashed line, and in the light look the sun is brighter than its sky and his stars are round points.

Still open, and next on my list: in the light look the tree shows as a stain under the sleep card at night; on an ordinary iPhone the sun sets behind the gear; the month-night stars are no stronger than bright ordinary ones; and the daytime moon is a faint flat disc. A second independent check of this build has not run yet.

better.title: Better drawn
better.sub: The same picture, drawn with more care. Round two is on the left of each pair and this build on the right. Tap either to enlarge it.

groups.title: The tree in leaf
groups.note: The crowns were flat clumps in three tones. Each leaf is now one small mark on a twig the tree already has, and the leaves gather into rounded masses of unequal size with sky between them. Shown fourteen minutes before sunset, as it stands beside the cards on the closed Duo.

groups.title: The clouds
groups.note: Round two’s clouds were one recipe: a flat hat. They are now quiet banks, each with a contour set by hand, lightest along the top and with no drawn base, held close to the tone of the sky behind them. Shown at 4:10 p.m. over the open Duo with the cards away.

groups.title: Light on the land
groups.note: Mist now lies along a crest as a thin torn layer instead of filling a hollow to a level. In the light look the hills are told apart by warm and cool, not by darker and lighter. The dull brown band behind the tree at dusk is an ember line rising through plum.

groups.title: The river
groups.note: The pinched waist is gone, the reeds are two clumps leaning downstream, the far bank is reflected as soft ribbons, and the moon’s path is scattered glints instead of a ladder of dashes.

pairs.label: The moon’s path, light, 9 p.m. before bedtime

groups.title: His stars, looking up
groups.note: The held bedtime frame with the cards away, three seconds in. His stars are laid out for the looked-up view, thicker overhead and thinning toward the land. The ring of light is now one soft band, and tonight’s star has a home of its own.

groups.title: The night, with the cards on
groups.note: This is the trade to judge. Round two came back down after the moment, so its night kept the tree in the strip with tonight’s star at its shoulder. Now the view stays up: the night is his stars, with tonight’s the large one, and the hill is out of sight until first light.

closing.title: About these mockups
points: These are stills and films from a browser mockup, not the app. Nothing in the app has changed. The films are stepped frame by frame, so they show the timing but not real performance.

Every legibility check passes on this build, all 143 of his stars are in view looking up on all three displays, and no event jumps on its first or last frame. A second independent review of this build has not run yet.
The Home screen is redrawn from the app with sample data, the glass tiles only approximate Liquid Glass, and the fonts are stand-ins.
The mockups use Chicago and a 2 July birthday as stand-ins. The app will use your daycare pin and his real date of birth.
Round two, as you last saw it, and today’s sky are below Painted for comparison. They follow the same look, display and hour.

page.filmSub: Bedtime and the opening, playing. Each film is the mockup stepped one frame at a time and joined, so the timing is as designed. It does not show how fast a phone will draw it.

skies.name: Painted
skies.line: The painted hill, better drawn, with a night that stays up until first light.
skies.idea: One illustrated land: a river valley on the left-hand page, a few big overlapping hills, a knoll, and one grown tree against the setting sun. At bedtime the view rises to a sky that holds one star for every night of his life, and stays there until first light.
works: Bedtime looks up once and stays. The cards return over the sky, and the caption is gone before they arrive.
A feed in the night moves nothing, and no event jumps on its first or last frame: 288 of 288 measured pairs.
All 143 of his stars are in view looking up, on all three displays.
Tonight’s star has a place of its own with the cards on, travels there with the view, and keeps a patch of dark sky round it on the way.
The clouds are quiet banks in the same hand as the hills, and nothing in the strip reads as a status symbol.
The tree in leaf is rounded masses of small leaves, and in summer it no longer shows past the sleep card when Home looks up.
notyet: With the cards on, the night is stars and no land. The hill and the tree are out of sight until first light.
With the cards on at night, the closed Duo and an ordinary iPhone never show the moon’s disc.
In the light look at night the tree shows as a stain under the sleep card.
On an ordinary iPhone the sun sets behind the gear, so the tree against the low sun exists only on the Duo.
The month-night stars are no stronger than bright ordinary ones, and the daytime moon is a faint flat disc.
In the dark look by day the clouds are very quiet. They may be too faint to read as weather.
The motion has only been seen as films stepped frame by frame, never at a phone’s own frame rate.
skies.build: No shader: one tall sky image, five layers of land and a pre-drawn tree on a SwiftUI Canvas. Looking up only slides those layers. Whether Home looks up is worked out from the clock, the sun and the sleep log, so nothing is stored.
